title: Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin (Standard Babylonian version)
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.12, Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin (ed. T. D. N. Mitto), SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin, Standard Babylonian version: 175 of 180 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
Naram-Sin describes the enemy hordes created by the gods, his failure to consult the omens, the destruction of his armies, his despair, and the advice he leaves to future rulers: keep calm, guard the land, and do not go out to fight.

The Cuthaean Legend presents itself as an inscription of Naram-Sin, king of Akkad (23rd century BCE), written for his successors. Hordes of strange warriors invade his land; ignoring the omens he attacks them and suffers three defeats, and he learns to trust the gods and to wait. The Standard Babylonian version is the best preserved. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/12/SB/-) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 175 of the 180 lines of the eBL edition (97%), from 5 tablets in the British Museum: 1881,0204.219 (Nineveh), K.5640 (Nineveh), K.5418.A (Nineveh), K.8582 (Nineveh), K.21047 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 5 of the 180 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 20-21 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.67.A (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara)); 169-171 (no photograph in eBL: SU-1951.67.A (Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara)). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; * collated sign; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; << >> sign written in error by the scribe; / alternative readings; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (blank space) a space left by the scribe.

translation.text:
1[Open the foundation box and] read well the [s]tela
2Of all the hardships that Nar[am-Sin], son of Sargon, went through.
3(no English for this line in the eBL edition)
4Sargon, my father, passed away.
5After Sargon, [m]y fat[her], passed away,
6[(…) I became ru]ler of the land.
7[(…) When … day]s had passed,
8[(…) When … year]s had gone by,
9[The land … and] its way of thinking [chan]ged.
10[Against Enmerkar, a host …] its […] and rode.
11[He inquired of the] great god[s],
12[Ishtar, Ilab]a, Zababa, Annunitum,
13[Shullat, Hanish, Shamash] the warrior,
14[He summoned] and charged [diviners],
15[Seven extispicies on seven la]mbs he made,
16[He set up] holy [reed al]tars.
17[The diviners] spoke thus,
18[…]
19[…] pale of face […]
translation.scan_note: British Museum 1881,0204.219: obverse, column i, the tablet's own lines 1 to 19. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/12/SB/-) attributes SB 1-19 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: the obverse has two columns of about 18 and 21 lines. The reverse has a right column of about 17 lines and a worn left column of about 7. This matches eBL's o i 19, o ii 21, r iii 18, r iv 7. Ink 81-2-4,219 is on the obverse and the edge. On this tablet of lines 11, 13, 15-19 only one to three signs survive and lines 1-10, 12, 14 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. eBL gives no English for line(s) 3.

22No sooner had the great [go]ds [spoken thus],
23Enmerkar [became like a] corpse, Shamash [rendered] a harsh judgment on him.
24The judgment on him, the verdict …, his ghost, the gho[sts of …],
25The ghosts of his family, the ghosts of his offspring, the ghosts of his offspring’s offspring, O Shamash the warrior,
26Lord of Above and Below, the lord of the Anunna-gods, lord of the ghosts (of the dead)!
27It was that they drink muddy water and drink no clear water (in the netherworld).

28That his sagacity and weaponry captured, defeated, (slew) that host,
29(Enmerkar) did not write upon a stela, nor did he, for my benefit, leave one behind for me,
30He did not put forth his name, so I did not bless him.
31Troops with bodies of “cave birds,” humans with raven faces
32Did the great gods create,
33In the place they created (them), the gods were their cohabitants.
34Tiamat suckled them,
35Belet-ili their mother made (them) fair.
36Inside the mountain(s) they grew up, became adults, got their stature.
37Seven kings they were, allies, they were glorious in form,
386,000 were their troops.
39Anu-banini, their father was king; their mother (was named) queen Melili,
40Their eldest brother, their vanguard, was named Memanduh,
41Their second brother was named Medudu,
42Their third brother was named […]pish,
43Their fourth brother was named Tartadada,
44Their fifth [br]other was named Baldahdah,
45Their sixth brother was named Ahudanadih,
46Their [seve]nth brother was named Hurrukidu.

47They rode against the sacred mountains,
48A soldier apprehended them, they [s]mote their thighs.
49At the beginning of their advance, they ad[vance]d on Burushandar,
50The land of Burushandar, its entire extent, was dispersed,
51Puhlu was dispersed,
52Puranshu [was d]ispers[ed].
53[…] (Na)shhuhu, Ahhahu, … [(…)] …
54Lubbudu, Lulbu, Ummanmanda, Karana, Shubat-E[nlil],
55And Inner Subartu, all of them [were] disp[ersed].
56They dispersed the Sealand, th[ey] advan[ced] on Gutium,
57They dispersed Gutium, they advance[d] on Elam,
58They destroyed Elam, they arrived at the (sea)coast,
59They killed the people at the place of embarkation, threw (them) into the river,
60Dilmun, Magan, Meluhha, whatever (lands) are in the midst of the sea, ([were] dis[persed]).
61Seventeen kings with 90,000 troops
62Sided with them to support them.
63[I s]ummoned a soldier and charged him,
64I set [a dagg]er and a pin in his hand,
65“Stab with the d[agg]er, prick with the pin.
66“[I]f blood comes out, they are human like us.

67“[If] no blood comes out, they are evil fiend, fate, [phan]tom, demons, handiwork of Enlil.”
68(no English for this line in the eBL edition)
69The soldier brought back his report back to me,
70“I stabbed with the [dagg]er,
71“I pricked with the pin, and blood came out.”
72I summoned and charged diviners,
73Seven extispicies upon seven lambs I performed,
74I set up holy reed altars.
75I inquire[d] of the great gods,
76Ishtar, Ilaba, Zababa, Annunitu,
77Shullat, H[anish], Shamash the warrior.
78The latchke[y] of the great g[o]ds did not allow my going nor my vain intent.
79Speaking to myself, thus I said,
80“What lion undertook divination?
81“What wolf consulted a dream interpreter?
82“I will go, as I like, like a brigand,
83“I will cast off what belongs to the gods, I will hold fast (only) to myself!”
84When the first year had come,
85I sent out 120,000 troops against them, not one returned alive.
86When the second year arrived, I sent out 90,000 (troops against them, not one returned alive).
87When the third year arrived, I sent out 60,700 (troops against them, not one returned alive).
88I was confounded, bewildered, checked, anxious, in despair.
89Speaking to myself, thus I said,
90“What have I left for a reign?
91“I am a king who brings no well-being to his land,

94Fear of lions, death, fate, convulsions,
95Panic, ague, economic collapse, starvation,
96D[iseas]e, migraine, sleeplessness of every sort had come down here with them.
97Above, from heaven, a deluge having been decided,
98Below, from the depths, (…) a deluge being imminent,
99Lord Ea made ready to speak,

105With entreaty to Ea and with prayer to the great gods,
106[I m]ade the holy New Year libations,
107I pe[rform]ed correctly the holy commands.
108I summoned and ch[arge]d diviners,
109Seven extispicies upon seven lambs I performed,
110I set up holy reed altars.
111I inquired of the gr[ea]t [g]ods,

113Shullat, [Hanish, Shamash the warri]or.
114The div[iners spoke to m]e [thus],

145“Ten quarts of barley will fetch on[e shekel of sil]ver.

147The great gods carried them off as tribute,
148(Whereas) I laid n[o] hand on them to kill.

155Listen to the wording of this stela.

165Restrain your warriors, take care of your person.

167Though he … your livestock, go not nigh him,
